source.title: Compressed Computation is (probably) not Computation in Superposition
source.authors: Jai Bhagat; Sara Molas-Medina; Giorgi Giglemiani; S. Heimersheim

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure values are not available as text, and the code URL is referred to but not printed.
record.tranche_reason: The study re-examines a toy model presented as computation in superposition and argues that its apparent advantage is caused by a mixing term in the labels, not superposition. It refines the interpretation of this toy-model evidence rather than reproducing the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.gate_note: The tested subject is the Compressed Computation toy model, which computes ReLU functions, not the original toy model of sparse features. The study reports results on its overcomplete sparse-input behavior and weight representation, but does not measure pairwise feature angles or establish near-orthogonality. It also reports dense-regime behavior, which is not evidence about sparse-feature superposition.
record.test_reason: The study asks whether the Compressed Computation toy model shows computation in superposition: computing 100 ReLU functions with 50 neurons. That is a related but different construct from every listed version. V1 concerns how sparse features are stored as nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, with a sparsity transition and regular geometry. The study measures loss against a naive baseline under different label-mixing matrices, and how neuron directions align with the mixing matrix's eigen- and singular subspaces. It never measures feature geometry, angles, interference or a storage phase transition. It also does not study polysemanticity, LLMs, SAEs or feature dimensionality. Its findings go under fits_no_version, not as tests of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the noise-induced mixing matrix, not computation in superposition, lets the CC model beat the naive baseline. They also explicitly rule out the idea that the noise matters only for training dynamics. The SNMF baseline explains some but not all of the model's performance and properties. They describe CC as probably not a suitable toy model of computation in superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study simplifies the Compressed Computation residual architecture to a one-layer MLP trained on ReLU(x) + Mx, and compares it with the Toy Models of Superposition claim rather than reproducing that original method.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on the mixing matrix and its magnitude: M = 0 removes the sparse-regime advantage, and loss decreases with σ for σ ≲ 0.03 before increasing at larger σ. The appendix also reports distinct sparse and dense solution regimes depending on input sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: The CC toy model's apparent ability to compute 100 ReLUs with 50 neurons depends on a noise-induced mixing term in the labels. With M=0 the model does not beat the naive loss, and fine-tuning on M=0 immediately reverts it to the naive loss. The gain grows with σ up to about 0.03.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Computation in superposition: toy networks can compute more nonlinear functions than they have neurons when inputs are sparse. The CC model is not evidence for this, because its advantage comes from label mixing.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained neuron read/write directions concentrate in the top-50 eigen- or singular subspace of the mixing matrix. Wout·Win correlates with M, and in the sparse regime each feature is represented by neuron combinations to about 70%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the CC setup, learned weights are governed by the mixing matrix rather than by superposed feature computation.

fits_no_version.finding: In the dense regime the model represents half the features with one neuron each and uses an output offset for the rest. A hand-coded naive-plus-offset solution matches it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The dense-regime advantage of the CC model is explained by a bias-like offset, not by superposition.

record.code_released: not stated; the text says core code and scripts are available at a URL but does not include the URL
record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Workshop: Mechanistic Interpretability
record.problems: The clean-label naive baseline is specified as 0.0833, but the authors note it is only valid for M = 0 and do not investigate an adjusted naive baseline for noisy labels. Most plotted loss values and alignment values are not given numerically in the text. The study does not directly measure pairwise feature angles or test whether feature directions are nearly orthogonal.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Dense-regime results are included in R10 but not linked to a claim version because that regime is not sparse-feature superposition.

untested.parts: All parts: feature storage as nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, the sparsity-dependent phase transition, and regular geometry. The study addresses computation in superposition, not representational geometry.
All parts: no test of neuron polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
All parts: no test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
All parts: no LLMs or dictionary learning.
All parts: feature dimensionality is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to V1 because 'superposition' appears in the title. The study's construct, however, is computation in superposition in Braun et al.'s CC model, which no listed version covers. The reader's challenges and limits_scope labels on V1 are therefore removed. If the claim gains a computation-in-superposition version, this study would be a T5 challenge to the CC evidence for it. The naive baseline of 0.0833 holds only for clean labels, and the authors do not compute an adjusted baseline for noisy labels. No numeric loss values are given in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests whether the Compressed Computation model’s sparse-input, overcomplete behavior is evidence of superposition. It does not directly measure pairwise angles between feature directions or establish the regular geometry described in the version.
Neuron polysemanticity and whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share them are not tested.
The study does not investigate polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
No LLM representations, neuron spread, or dictionary recovery are studied.
No SAE features or claims about their completeness, stability, or canonical status are studied.
The study examines neuron read/write directions and matrix subspaces, but does not test whether the represented features themselves are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: 1-layer MLP model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated sparse-input loss with M = 0 and compared it with the naive baseline.
rows.measure: Loss relative to the naive baseline
rows.baseline: 0.0833 loss for the naive baseline on a clean dataset
rows.value: The model does not beat the naive loss for sparse inputs.
rows.note: The authors argue that if the advantage came from computation in superposition, it should persist with M = 0. The naive baseline value is specified for the clean dataset.
rows.check: Loss vs naive baseline with M=0 bears on computation in superposition in the CC model, not on V1 feature storage geometry. The state 'absent' refers to the CC advantage, not to any listed version.

rows.subject: 1-layer MLP model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated loss with embedding-like mixing matrix.

conditions.value: high sparsity; exact p not stated

rows.measure: Loss relative to the naive baseline
rows.baseline: 0.0833 naive loss is shown for comparison; the text cautions that this baseline applies only to the clean dataset
rows.value: The model beats the naive loss; embedding-like M allows the lowest loss among the stated M conditions.
rows.note: The authors attribute the gain to the mixing term. Exact loss values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Beating the naive loss with embedding-like M concerns the CC computation advantage, not V1. The naive baseline is valid only for M=0, so the comparison is not a clean measure.

rows.subject: 1-layer MLP model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated loss with random mixing matrix.

conditions.value: high sparsity; exact p not stated

rows.measure: Loss relative to the naive baseline
rows.baseline: 0.0833 naive loss is shown for comparison; the text cautions that this baseline applies only to the clean dataset
rows.value: The model beats the naive loss; random M behaves similarly to the embedding-like M.
rows.note: The authors state that the performance profile is reproduced by this random M. Exact loss values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Same as R2: this is the CC advantage under random M ~ N(0, 0.02), not V1 storage geometry.

rows.subject: 1-layer MLP model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated loss with symmetric random mixing matrix.

conditions.value: symmetric random M; distribution not stated
high sparsity; exact p not stated

rows.measure: Loss profile compared with the reported Compressed Computation results
rows.value: The symmetric random M matrix matches Braun et al.’s results almost exactly; with nonzero M, the model beats the naive loss at high sparsity.
rows.note: The text does not give numerical loss values for this condition.
rows.check: Same as R2. The symmetric random M distribution is not stated, and no numeric value is given.

rows.subject: 1-layer MLP model
rows.operation_detail: Varied the magnitude of a random mixing matrix and measured optimal loss.
rows.measure: Optimal loss as a function of σ
rows.baseline: σ = 0 condition shown in Figure 2 right; exact value not stated
rows.value: Loss decreases with σ for σ ≲ 0.03.
rows.note: The text says loss increases again at large σ, but gives no exact loss values.
rows.check: Loss as a function of the mixing magnitude σ is not a V1 measure. The trend is read from Figure 2 right; no numbers are given in the text.

rows.subject: 1-layer MLP model
rows.operation_detail: Varied the magnitude of a random mixing matrix and measured optimal loss.

conditions.value: large σ; exact range not stated

rows.measure: Optimal loss as a function of σ
rows.baseline: Lower loss at small σ, for σ ≲ 0.03
rows.value: Loss increases again at large σ.
rows.note: The increase at large σ is described qualitatively; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: 'Reversed' is wrong: a rise in loss at large σ is not the opposite of any version's effect. It is part of the same σ curve as R5 and could be merged with it.

rows.subject: 1-layer MLP model
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned a model trained with nonzero M on a dataset with M = 0.
rows.measure: Loss relative to the naive baseline
rows.baseline: Loss before fine-tuning on M = 0; exact value not stated
rows.value: The model immediately reverts to the naive loss.
rows.note: The authors use this result to argue that the lower loss depends on the mixing term, not merely on training dynamics.
rows.check: The fine-tuning transplant to M=0 tests whether the CC advantage depends on the mixing term. It does not test V1.

rows.subject: trained Compressed Computation model
rows.operation_detail: Measured how neuron read/write directions relate to eigenvector and singular-vector subspaces.

conditions.value: embedding-induced M and the corresponding I + M analysis; separate exact matrix conditions not fully specified in the text

rows.measure: Alignment of neuron directions and Wout Win with matrix eigenvectors or singular vectors
rows.value: Neuron read/write directions lie mostly in the subspace associated with the positive eigenvalues of M or the top 50 singular vectors of I + M; similarity drops sharply around index 50, and the remaining directions are strongly attenuated.
rows.note: This is alignment to subspaces defined by the mixing matrix; it is not a measurement of pairwise angles among represented feature directions.
rows.check: This measures neuron alignment to the mixing-matrix subspaces, not pairwise feature geometry or near-orthogonality.

rows.subject: trained Compressed Computation model
rows.operation_detail: Examined how learned weights represent input features in the sparse-input solution.
rows.measure: Distribution of feature representation across neurons
rows.value: Weights are distributed across all features; combinations of neurons represent each feature to around 70%.
rows.note: The description does not establish near-orthogonality of the represented features.
rows.check: About 70% feature representation by neuron combinations in the CC solution is a qualitative weight description. It does not measure superposition geometry as V1 defines it.

rows.subject: trained Compressed Computation model
rows.operation_detail: Examined the dense-regime solution and its response to one-hot inputs.
rows.baseline: Naive loss baseline; exact dense-regime loss not stated
rows.value: The model tends to implement half the input features with one neuron each and largely ignore the other half; it can beat the naive baseline in the dense regime.
rows.note: This concerns dense inputs, not sparse-feature superposition.
rows.check: This dense-regime result is correctly unlinked. The authors explain it with a naive solution plus an output offset (Appendix D).

rows.subject: SNMF baseline
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated weights derived from the semi-non-negative matrix factorization of M.
rows.measure: Loss profile compared with the trained model and naive baseline
rows.baseline: Naive baseline and trained Compressed Computation model
rows.value: Beats the naive loss for a range of noise scales and qualitatively matches the trained model’s loss profile, but does not reach as low a loss as the trained model.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a baseline derived from the mixing matrix alone; its result does not directly test the named feature-geometry versions.
rows.check: This is the study's own hand-coded SNMF baseline compared with the trained model, i.e. its own method's performance. It should not be a result row on the claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Sparse-input Compressed Computation model with M = 0
reader_labels.reason: The model does not beat the naive loss for sparse inputs in this clean condition, contrary to the authors’ stated expectation if the apparent advantage arose from computation in superposition (R1, R7). This does not establish that superposition generally fails.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Sparse-input Compressed Computation model with nonzero mixing M
reader_labels.reason: The apparent sparse-regime advantage occurs with nonzero M, scales with its magnitude over part of the tested range, and is attributed by the authors to mixing rather than to superposition (R2–R6, R8). The study does not directly measure near-orthogonal feature geometry.
